procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
Madras High Court: M. Selvakumar filed Writ Petition (c) No. 18705 of 2010 challenging the order of the Tribunal. The Division Bench of Madras High Court allowed the writ petition on 24.01.2012.
Delhi High Court: The Respondent challenged the order of the Tribunal by filing a Writ Petition (c) No. 7377 of 2013. The High Court allowed the writ petition on 13.10.2014, setting aside the order of the Tribunal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Union of India filed SLP (c) No. 21587 of 2013 against the Madras High Court judgment dated 24.01.2012. The Union Public Service Commission filed an appeal challenging the Delhi High Court judgment dated 13.10.2014. The Supreme Court stayed the operation of the Delhi High Court judgment on 08.07.2015.

directions: The judgment of the Madras High Court dated 24.1.2012 in M. Selvakumar versus Central Administrative Tribunal and Others is set aside and the Writ Petition is dismissed.
The judgment of Delhi High Court dated 13.10.2014 impugned in the last two appeals is set aside and the Writ Petition filed by the respondents is hereby dismissed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court cannot interfere with governmental policy unless the policy is absolutely capricious, not informed by reason, totally arbitrary, or offends the basic requirements of Article 14 of the Constitution. It is not within the domain of the courts to assess whether a particular public policy is wise or if a better policy could be evolved.
obiter: As long as a declaration of law by a higher court stands and is not set aside, a lower tribunal ought to follow it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the rules governing horizontal reservation and relaxation, including the number of examination attempts for Physically Handicapped candidates, are a matter of governmental policy. The judiciary's role is not to assess the wisdom of such policies or to devise better alternatives. Judicial interference is only warranted if a policy is proven to be absolutely capricious, devoid of reason, or so arbitrary that it violates the fundamental principles of Article 14 of the Constitution, a standard the respondents failed to meet.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for judicial review of a policy decision: The Court can only interfere if the policy framed is absolutely capricious and non-informed by reasons, or totally arbitrary, offending the basic requirement of the Article 14 of the Constitution.
why_respondent_won: The horizontal reservation and relaxation for Physically Handicapped Category candidates for Civil Services Examination is a matter of Governmental policy.
It is not in the domain of the courts to embark upon an inquiry as to whether a particular public policy is wise and acceptable or whether better policy could be evolved.

The Court can only interfere if the policy framed is absolutely capricious and non-informed by reasons, or totally arbitrary, offending the basic requirement of the Article 14 of the Constitution, and the respondents' challenge did not meet this high threshold.
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the principle of judicial restraint in matters of public policy, stating that the executive branch is responsible for formulating such policies after considering relevant materials, and the judiciary should not overstep its domain by questioning the wisdom of those policies.
